newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN describes last hours of Najibullah's life.
newsitem.headline: UN describes last hours of Najibullah's life.

text.p: Two days before former Afghan president Najibullah was taken out of the U.N. compound, shot in the head and hung on a tower by Taleban militia, he was offered a move elsewhere but refused.
"He repeatedly rejected suggestions that he might be moved and said he felt safer in the compound," chief U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa told reporters.

No particular site was discussed but the United Nations was willing to ask the tottering Afghan government to help him get out of the compound as the radical Taleban Islamic militia began to take strategic areas around the city. U.N. staff were living in a house 10 minutes from the compound.
Nevertheless, Najibullah telephoned U.N. officials on Thursday, saying all government soldiers had disappeared.

"But there was nothing we could do," Foa said. "We don't have any troops, we don't have guns. We called around, talked to the Red Cross but there was nothing anyone could do to get there. There was total chaos in the city."

Najibullah led a Moscow-backed government in Afghanistan for six years and was ousted on April 16, 1992, by Moslem Mujahedeen, who refused to let him leave the country and join his family in India. He sought refuge behind the walls of U.N. headquarters in Kabul, an unwilling recluse.
The government's troops guarded the gates of the U.N. office building to make sure he could not escape but also promised the United Nations to protect him.
Foa said only one person remained in the compound after government troops fled, an unarmed Afghan watchman.
At 1:40 a.m. local time on Friday, five armed men walked through they gates, brushing past the nightwatchman and went straight to Najibullah's rooms.
"They evidently knew exactly where he was," Foa said. "They sat down and talked to him for several minutes and then took him away by force."

She said U.N. officials believed he was shot in the head while his younger brother, Shahpur Ahmadzai, died from hanging. The bodies of both men were seen by witnsses in Kabul hanging from a tower used as a traffic post at the gates of the presidential palace before jeering crowds.

At about 6 a.m. she said the militia returned again and took away Najibullah's brother. The Taleban made a third visit two hours later and by this time two U.N. security officers had arrived. Despite protests, the militia searched the compound looking for Najibullah's companions, a bodyguard and a political advisor but both had fled, she said..

In the 1980s Najibullah was head of the secret police under the Soviet-backed regime of Babrak Karmel. He became president in 1986, a few years before Moscow ended its 10-year occupation of Afghanistan in February 1989.

Before he was ousted in 1992 U.N. officials he had offered to resign as part of a peace process. In return, he was allowed to leave the country but as he was driving to the airport he was stopped by Afghan army officers and sought sanctuary in the U.N. compound.

Foa said that Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali deplored "the terrible loss of life in the battle for Kabul and he found it particularly regretful that a person who has sought sanctuary in U.N. presmises was abducted which is a breach of the inviobility of U.N. premises."

The chief U.N. respresentative in Afghanistan, Nobert Hull of Germany, said in a statement that the abduction and killing were "without any legitimate judicial procedure" constituted a grave violation of the immunity (U.N.) premises enjoyed under international law."
These acts "also further jeopardise all the efforts which are being made to secure a peaceful settlement of the Afghanistan conflict," Holl said.
